summary: Describes the NICNAME/WHOIS server and how to access it. With its database, it provides online directory look-up equivalent to the ARPANET Directory. Replaced by RFC 954 and RFC 3912.

plainLanguage.summary: An online phone book you can ask about people and computers on the network. Newer rules have since replaced this one.

questions: how does the whois protocol work
subtitle: The original description of the NICNAME/WHOIS directory server on the SRI-NIC machine.

tldr.problem: ARPANET users needed an online way to look up the full name, address, telephone number and network mailbox of other users.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to port 43 on SRI-NIC, sends one command line ending in a carriage return and line feed, reads the reply, and the server then closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: The replies are meant for human readers, not machines. The RFC was replaced by RFC 954 and RFC 3912.

today: RFC 812 has been obsoleted by RFC 954 and RFC 3912, which replace this description of the service.

sections.title: A Network Directory Service
sections.content:
The NICNAME/WHOIS server runs on the SRI-NIC machine and gives ARPANET users a directory look-up. Together with the Identification Data Base it is equivalent to the ARPANET Directory. It delivers the full name, U.S. mailing address, telephone number and network mailbox of users, and DCA strongly encourages hosts to give their users access.

DCA asks each individual with a directory on an ARPANET host to be registered, by sending their details by electronic mail to NIC@SRI-NIC.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a phone book for people on the network. If you are in the book, others can find how to reach you.

sections.title: The Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol is similar to NAME/FINGER (RFC 742). A client connects to the service host SRI-NIC on TCP service port 43 decimal, sends a single command line ending in <CRLF>, and receives the answer. The server closes the connection as soon as its output is finished.

NICNAME is the global name of the user program, though some sites call it WHOIS. Versions existed for Tenex, Tops-20 and Unix, and the RFC advises using the NIC-supplied programs because the protocol will continue to evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: You make one call, ask one question, hear the answer, and the line hangs up on its own.

sections.title: Command Lines and Replies
sections.content:
A command line is normally one name specification. Sending a lone ? returns help text listing the accepted formats. A leading period forces a name-only search, a leading exclamation point forces a handle-only search, and ending with ... matches anything from that point. An asterisk before the argument asks for the entire membership list of a group or organization.

The replies are not intended to be machine-readable; they are passed straight to a human user. The RFC shows a search for dyer that lists four people, and a search for mary that shows one full record with an address and phone number.
sections.plainLanguage: You can type part of a name, or add a special mark to say you only want names, or only IDs. The answer is written for people to read.
